# Science losing its way: examples from the realm of microbial N 2 -fixation in cereals and other non-legumes

## Abstract

### Background

Despite more than 50 years of research, no robust evidence suggests that inoculation of cereals and other non-legumes with free-living and/or endophytic bacteria leads to fixation of agronomically significant quantities of dinitrogen gas (N 2) from the atmosphere. A plethora of new products claims to increase the growth and yields of major cereals and other crops through stimulating N 2 -fixation by inoculating with bacteria.

### Scope

We review the literature on N 2 -fixation by bacteria in the rhizosphere and as endophytes in non-legume plants. We find no unequivocal evidence that these bacteria fix agriculturally significant amounts of N 2 from the atmosphere in non-legumes. Research since the 1930s has followed repeated, overlapping cycles that have concluded that plant-growth-promoting hormones were the primary reason for crop response to microbial inoculants.

### Conclusion

We contend that regulations are required to prevent the sale of inoculant products with unsubstantiated and spurious claims. Such regulations should require that unequivocal evidence is provided and independently verified, that: (i) the inoculant bacterium can fix N 2 from the atmosphere (i.e. that it possesses all the genes required to make nitrogenase), (ii) it has a clear mechanism to protect nitrogenase from poisoning by free oxygen, (iii) the bacterium is present in sufficient numbers throughout the growth cycle of the plant, (iv) that enhanced respiration can be detected from the putative N 2 -fixing tissues, (v) that inoculation of the non-legume growing in an N-free medium leads to prolific growth and accumulation of nitrogen, and (vi) more than one method is used to confirm quantitatively significant inputs from N 2 -fixation in the field.

## Introduction

Growing concerns about the effect of intensive agricultural practices on climate change, human health, biodiversity and soil degradation have led to increased interest in alternatives to agrochemicals to provide nutrients and protect against pests and diseases (Giller et al. 2021). In particular, there is renewed interest in using beneficial microbes to promote plant growth by producing phytohormones, increasing biotic and abiotic stress tolerance, acting as biocontrol agents, and supplying or increasing the uptake of nutrients (Andrade et al. 2023; Santos et al. 2019). We do not dispute that positive responses to inoculation with some microbes are observed, but claims that inoculants containing N 2 -fixing bacteria can supply a large proportion of the N required by cereals and other non-legume crops lack any robust scientific basis. While such supposed N 2 -fixing inoculants have become a major industry, we show that this has run well ahead of any credible evidence.

We recognize that the example of scientific misinformation concerning N 2 -fixing bacteria and cereal crops is not an isolated case. Indeed, the rapid expansion of the research industry in recent decades has led to an increasing fraction of published research being shown to be misleading or not repeatable (West and Bergstrom 2021), with red flags being raised in the medical (Heen and Vogt 2024), agriculture (Edmeades 2011), soil science and agronomy (Frank and Husted 2024) and psychology (Kravitz and Mitroff 2023) fields, to name a few. The problem is equally apparent in what are considered both lesser and quality journals (e.g. Van Noorden 2023).

The critical scientific method hinges on Karl Popper’s Theory of Falsification – of deriving a hypothesis, then trying to disprove it through experimentation, rejecting the hypothesis if it does not stand up to scrutiny. Yet in much contemporary research it seems that scientists have moved away from this approach in favour of accumulating evidence to support a phenomenon or mechanism that they believe to be true. However, a fact is not something which one can find evidence to support, but rather a hypothesis that is yet to be proven false. Shifts in scientific paradigms occur only when a sufficient body of evidence emerges from detailed, robust investigations that challenge current understanding (Kuhn 1970). In this paper we argue for a return to Popper’s approach by exploring a number of examples of research on N 2 -fixation associated with cereals and other non-legumes where there were no attempts to disprove a hypothesis.

Before we discuss specific examples of unsubstantiated claims of N 2 -fixation in non-legumes, it is worthwhile to consider the process of biological N 2 -fixation and the conditions that enable it to occur.

## Nitrogen-fixing organisms

Nitrogenase, the only enzyme which converts atmospheric dinitrogen (N 2) gas to ammonia, is a prokaryotic (microbial) enzyme found in both the Archaea and the Eubacteria. Three forms of nitrogenase exist which contain different metals (molybdenum, vanadium or iron); these can all be traced back to a single, highly conserved evolutionary enzymic pathway (Mus et al. 2018). Given that nitrogenase evolved in the primaeval soup – more than 2.5 billion years ago (Parsons et al. 2021) – it is remarkable that no eukaryote has evolved the ability to fix N 2 gas independently. The reduction of N 2 to ammonia requires a lot of energy to break the very stable triple bond, yet a common feature of all nitrogenase enzymes is that they are irreversibly denatured in the presence of oxygen. This presents a conundrum: How can aerobic respiration be maintained to produce the energy needed to fix N 2 while protecting the nitrogenase from oxygen? This is called the oxygen paradox of N 2 -fixation, and several different mechanisms have evolved to allow bacteria to fix N 2 without nitrogenase being exposed to oxygen.

### Solving the oxygen paradox

The most effective and economically important N 2 -fixing symbiosis is undoubtedly the association of legumes with rhizobia. Legumes form structures known as nodules on their roots in response to signals from the rhizobia. The rhizobia colonise cells in the centre of the nodule (the infected zone) and differentiate into ‘bacteroids’, which are present within the cytoplasm of the infected cells but encapsulated in structures (symbiosomes) by a membrane of plant origin, known as the peribacteroid membrane. The nodule medulla is surrounded by a zone of densely packed tissue that forms a barrier to the diffusion of oxygen. This barrier restricts oxygen diffusion so that the concentration of free oxygen in the intercellular spaces in the centre of the nodule is very low. The active respiration of the N 2 -fixing bacteroids uses up oxygen rapidly, which is why an oxygen carrier is required. Leghaemoglobin, which gives the nodules their pink colour, has a high affinity for oxygen and acts as an extremely efficient carrier, transporting oxygen from the intercellular spaces to the N 2 -fixing bacteroids. Thus, the oxygen diffusion barrier and leghaemoglobin combine to ensure that nitrogenase is not exposed to oxygen while providing sufficient oxygen to support active aerobic respiration and provide the energy required for the bacteroids to fix N 2 (Giller 2001).

Different mechanisms of oxygen protection are found in other symbioses and associative N 2 -fixation (Santi et al. 2013). N 2 -fixation in the actinorhizal symbioses takes place in nodules formed on the roots of higher plants, which are colonised by filamentous actinobacteria classified as Frankia. Within the nodules, the bacteria form thick-walled vesicles, which have a very low permeability to oxygen and are the site of active N 2 -fixation. In filamentous cyanobacteria, such as Nostoc and Anabaena, N 2 -fixation takes place in specialised thick-walled cells known as heterocysts that are almost impermeable to oxygen.

Some N 2 -fixing bacteria are strictly anaerobic (e.g. Clostridium) and cannot grow in the presence of oxygen. Others are facultative anaerobes, which can only fix N 2 when the soil becomes anaerobic (e.g. Klebsiella). A number of mechanisms exist whereby bacteria can fix N 2 under low oxygen tension (i.e. microaerophilic conditions). For example, Derxia gummosa, as its name suggests, produces a dense gum on artificial media that restricts oxygen diffusion so that it is used up rapidly enough that nitrogenase is never exposed to free oxygen – a process referred to as ‘respiratory protection’. A different adaptation is found in Azotobacter vinelandii, which is able to prevent its nitrogenase from coming into contact with oxygen by what is termed ‘conformational protection’: in essence, a folding of the enzyme under fully aerobic conditions. Species of Azospirillum cultivated in the laboratory on semi-solid media form ‘pellicles’ beneath the surface and fix N 2 microaerophilically (Giller 2001).

N 2 -fixing bacteria can be found as free-living bacteria in soil or associated with plants (Table 1). They can be found on the surface of plant leaves (epiphytic), in large numbers close to plant roots in what is termed the rhizosphere, or within the plant tissues as ‘endophytes’. A wide range of bacteria also form symbioses with eukaryotes, which are intimate, mutualistic associations in which the cells of the plant are colonised by the bacteria (see Sect. 2.2 below). Cyanobacteria form intimate symbiotic associations with fungi (lichens) as well as a number of plants including ferns (Azolla) and some higher plants (e.g. Gunnera, cycads). A wide range of bacterial genera are able to colonise root nodules on legumes and fix N 2 symbiotically (Table 1). Filamentous actinomycetes classified as Frankia also colonise root nodules of a range of genera of higher plants. The enrichment of N 2 -fixing bacteria such as Azospirillum spp. in the rhizosphere of certain tropical grasses compared to the bulk soil led to these being referred to as “associative symbioses”, although whether the term symbiosis applies is questioned given that these are rather loose associations (Giller 2001).

### Evidence of ‘symbioses’ of N 2 -fixing bacteria and non-legumes.

Many bacteria colonise the rhizospheres of plants and some colonise the plants endophytically. Some of these root-associated and endophytic bacteria are able to fix N 2, but simply demonstrating the presence of a bacterium, or showing that it fixes N 2 in situ, does not prove that agronomically significant amounts of N are captured. As we now know from numerous microbiome/ metagenomics studies, the plant microbiome is both enormous and exceptionally diverse e.g. that of sugarcane (Souza et al. 2016). The microbiome can be loosely divided into rhizospheric, epiphytic and endophytic, with diversity generally declining from the bulk (non-rhizospheric) soil towards the plant interior, suggesting that the plant has some control on which organisms can actually enter its root tissues (Turner et al. 2013). The microbiome/metagenomics data also illustrate that older methods to isolate and culture bacteria using so-called “selective” media inevitably biased perceptions enormously towards the few bacterial taxa that are amenable to culture, and completely overlooked the vast majority of bacteria that are so far unculturable.
